groups.high: GDPR Article 33 requires a controller to notify the competent supervisory authority of a personal data breach without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of awareness, unless the breach is unlikely to risk individuals' rights and freedoms. If notification occurs later, give reasons for delay. Do not wait for a complete investigation: information can be supplied in phases without undue further delay. Describe the breach, relevant categories and approximate numbers of people and records, likely consequences, mitigation measures and a contact point. A processor must inform the controller without undue delay. Document all breaches, including reasons for deciding not to notify. Article 34 separately requires communication to affected individuals without undue delay when high risk is likely, subject to exceptions such as effective protective encryption or disproportionate effort requiring public communication. Article 33 and 34 infringements can attract the Article 83(4) maximum of €10 million or, for an undertaking, 2% of worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher. A maximum fine is not automatic; other infringements may have different ceilings.
groups.mid: GDPR Article 33 tells a controller what to do after a personal data breach. Report to the proper supervisory authority without undue delay. Where feasible, do this within 72 hours after you become aware. You may not need to report if risk to people's rights and freedoms is unlikely. If late, say why. Do not wait until every fact is known. Send details in stages without further undue delay. Say what happened, who and what records were affected, and the likely harm. Give approximate numbers, actions taken and a contact point. A processor must tell the controller without undue delay. Record every breach and why you did or did not report it. Article 34 separately says to tell affected people without undue delay when high risk is likely. There are exceptions. Effective encryption may protect the data. Public notice may replace direct contact if that takes disproportionate effort. Under Article 83(4), these failures can face up to €10 million or 2% of the undertaking's prior-year worldwide turnover, whichever is higher. This is a maximum, not an automatic fine. Other breaches may have other limits.
groups.low: GDPR Article 33 applies after a personal data breach. The controller must report to the proper supervisory authority without undue delay. Where feasible, report within 72 hours of awareness. If risk to people's rights and freedoms is unlikely, a report may not be needed. If late, explain why. Do not wait for a full investigation. Send details in stages without further undue delay. Say what happened and the likely harm. Give the types and approximate numbers of people and records affected. Say what steps you took and provide a contact point. A processor must tell the controller without undue delay. Record every breach. Say why it was or was not reported. Article 34 separately deals with telling affected people. Do this without undue delay if high risk is likely. Exceptions can apply. Effective encryption may have made the data safe. If direct contact takes too much effort for the case, a public notice may be needed. Article 83(4) sets the maximum for these failures. It can be €10 million. For an undertaking, it can instead be 2% of prior-year worldwide turnover if higher. This is a maximum, not an automatic fine. Other breaches may have other limits.
groups.source_review: Checked EDPB breach guidance and GDPR Article33/34 distinction; EUR-Lex direct HTML bot challenge encountered.
groups.notes: Qualified 72-hour feasible provision, added phased notification/processor duty and Article34 exceptions; no automatic cap application.

groups.high: India's Right to Information Act 2005 generally requires the Public Information Officer to decide a request within 30 days under section 7(1), either supplying information or rejecting it with reasons under the Act. Information concerning life or liberty must be provided within 48 hours. Applications through an Assistant Public Information Officer can add five days; this is not a general extension for complexity. Transfers to another public authority should occur within five days. Third-party consultation and specified fee-payment periods have their own timing rules. Failure to decide in time is deemed refusal, and eligible delayed information must be supplied free of charge. Under section 20, the Central or State Information Commission may impose ₹250 per day up to ₹25,000 for specified failures without reasonable cause, including delay or wrongful refusal, after giving the officer a reasonable opportunity to be heard. The penalty is not automatically billed on day 31. The officer bears the burden of showing reasonable and diligent conduct. Appeal or complaint routes and possible disciplinary recommendations are distinct from the personal fine. A universal three-day acknowledgement duty or section 14 penalty rule is not established here.
groups.mid: India's Right to Information Act 2005 sets time limits for requests. Section 7(1) usually gives the Public Information Officer 30 days. The officer must give the facts or refuse with reasons allowed by law. A request about life or liberty needs information within 48 hours. An Assistant Public Information Officer can add five days to the route. This is not a general 35-day limit for hard requests. A transfer to another public body should take no more than five days. Third-party checks and some fee-payment periods have their own rules. No decision in time counts as refusal. Delayed information must be free where the Act says so. Section 20 covers fines for set failures without good reason. The Central or State Information Commission may fine the officer ₹250 a day, up to ₹25,000. It is not an automatic bill on day 31. The officer gets a chance to explain. The officer must show that they acted with care and good reason. Appeals and complaints are separate routes. Discipline may also be recommended. There is no general rule to acknowledge all requests in three days. Section 14 is not the fine rule.
groups.low: India's Right to Information Act 2005 gives time limits. Section 7(1) usually allows 30 days for a decision. The Public Information Officer must give the facts. Or they must say why the law allows refusal. If life or liberty is at stake, give information within 48 hours. An Assistant Public Information Officer can add five days. A hard request alone does not allow 35 days. A transfer to another public body should take at most five days. Checks with third parties have their own timing rules. So do some fee-payment periods. No answer in time counts as refusal. The Act can require late information to be free. Section 20 allows a personal fine for set failures without good reason. The Central or State Information Commission may set it. It is ₹250 a day. The cap is ₹25,000. It is not automatic on day 31. The officer can explain. They must show they acted with care. Appeals and complaints are separate. The Commission may also recommend action under staff rules. There is no general rule to say all requests were received within three days. Section 14 does not set the fine.
groups.source_review: Checked India Post official RTI guidance and Act identity; India Code PDF retrieval timed out. Statutory distinctions stated, not case-specific appeal advice.
groups.notes: Corrected false3day acknowledgement, complexity extension, section14 citation and automatic strict-liability fine.

groups.high: Canada's historical federal carbon-pricing schedule used CAD 80 per tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2024 and planned annual CAD 15 increases to CAD 170 in 2030. These figures must be dated: they do not describe an unchanged present-day consumer fuel tax. The federal government set fuel-charge rates to zero from 1 April 2025 and removed the requirement for provinces and territories to maintain consumer-facing carbon pricing. Industrial carbon pricing remained a separate policy mechanism, including the federal Output-Based Pricing System and provincial systems. Carbon pricing creates an incentive to reduce emissions by attaching a cost to pollution; it encourages, rather than deters, abatement. The effect depends on coverage, exemptions, rebates, technology and demand, not a guarantee that all fossil-fuel production becomes uncompetitive at one price. Industrial output-based systems use performance standards and compliance units rather than simply charging every tonne identically. Historical household rebates and revenue arrangements must not be presented as continuing automatically after the consumer charge ceased. Check the relevant year, jurisdiction and current industrial rules before using a rate for planning.
groups.mid: Canada's old federal plan put a price of CAD 80 per tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent on pollution in 2024. It planned CAD 15 rises each year to CAD 170 in 2030. These are figures from that plan, not an unchanged tax on consumers today. From 1 April 2025, federal fuel-charge rates became zero. Provinces and territories no longer had to keep a consumer-facing carbon price. Prices for industrial pollution are a separate system. These include the federal Output-Based Pricing System and provincial plans. A pollution price aims to make cuts in emissions more worthwhile. It does not aim to stop those cuts. The effect depends on coverage, exceptions, rebates, technology and demand. One price does not make all fossil-fuel work unable to compete. Industrial output-based systems use performance standards and compliance units, not one flat charge on every tonne. Old household rebates did not have to continue unchanged. Check the date, place and current industrial rules before using a rate to plan.
groups.low: Canada had an old federal carbon-price plan. In 2024 it used CAD 80 per tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent. This is a unit for the warming caused by gases. The plan added CAD 15 each year. It aimed for CAD 170 in 2030. These figures refer to the old plan. Do not use them as an unchanged consumer tax today. From 1 April 2025, federal fuel-charge rates became zero. Provinces and territories no longer had to keep a carbon price paid by consumers. Pollution from large firms is priced in a separate way. One scheme is the federal Output-Based Pricing System. Provinces have their own schemes too. A price on pollution aims to make emissions cuts worthwhile. It is meant to encourage cuts, not stop them. Results depend on what is covered. So do exceptions and rebates. Tools in use and what people buy matter too. One price does not mean all fossil-fuel work cannot compete. The systems for large firms use output-based performance standards. They use compliance units, which are credits or payments used to meet rules. They do not put one flat charge on every tonne. Do not assume the old rebates to homes went on unchanged. Check the year and place first. Check the current rules for large firms before using a rate to plan.
groups.source_review: Checked historical schedule and official consumer-price removal effective2025. Current industrial details not treated as universal fixed rates.
groups.notes: Corrected outdated consumer-tax continuation, deterrence-of-abatement reversal and guaranteed sector outcome/rebate assumptions.

groups.high: FATF payment-transparency standards require relevant originator and beneficiary information to accompany covered transfers so institutions can trace payments and assess financial-crime risks. Originator means sender; beneficiary means intended recipient. Requirements depend on the transfer type, amount and national implementation. The USD/EUR 1,000 figure is not a universal exemption below which no information is needed: a permitted de minimis threshold can allow reduced information or verification for certain transfers, while suspicion can require further checks. Domestic transfers and card purchases have distinct rules. Virtual-asset requirements are addressed through Recommendation 15 and its interpretive framework as well as relevant Travel Rule standards. In June 2025 FATF revised Recommendation 16, including standardised information for peer-to-peer cross-border payments above USD/EUR 1,000 and fraud/error safeguards; implementation is due by the end of 2030. FATF sets international standards implemented by jurisdictions, not a directly enforceable global statute for every customer. No universal API, automatic block or suspicious-report outcome follows from this summary. Check the current local law, required fields, verification, recordkeeping and secure data-transfer duties.
groups.mid: The FATF Travel Rule helps show who sends and receives money. The sender is the originator. The intended recipient is the beneficiary. What data is needed depends on the transfer, amount and local law. USD/EUR 1,000 is not a rule saying no data is needed below that amount. Some transfers below a permitted threshold may use less data or fewer checks. Suspected crime may need more checks. Domestic transfers and card purchases have other rules. Virtual assets also use Recommendation 15 and its related rules. FATF changed Recommendation 16 in June 2025. Changes include standard data for peer-to-peer cross-border payments above USD/EUR 1,000. They also add safeguards against fraud and error. Implementation is due by the end of 2030. FATF sets standards that countries put into local law. It is not one global law for every customer. It does not demand one universal API or automatic blocking in every flagged case. Check local rules for data, identity checks, records and safe data transfer.
groups.low: The FATF Travel Rule helps trace covered transfers. It asks who sends money and who should get it. The originator is the sender. The beneficiary is the intended recipient. The data needed depends on the amount, transfer and local law. USD/EUR 1,000 is not a data-free line. Some smaller transfers may use less data or fewer checks. This depends on a permitted threshold. Suspected crime can need more checks. Domestic transfers have other rules. So do card purchases. Virtual assets also use Recommendation 15 and related rules. FATF changed Recommendation 16 in June 2025. One change covers standard data for peer-to-peer cross-border payments above USD/EUR 1,000. Others guard against fraud and error. The changes are due by the end of 2030. FATF sets standards. Countries put them into local law. It is not one global law applied to all customers. It does not demand one universal API. Nor does it mean every flagged transfer is blocked. Check local rules for data, identity checks, records and safe transfer of data.
groups.source_review: Checked FATF2025 revision and2030 implementation timing; threshold not treated as information-free exemption.
groups.notes: Corrected universal>$1000 data fields/API/direct-exchange/global-law claims, missing reduced requirements and timeline.

groups.high: For the 2025 Bundestag election, the five-percent threshold concerned a party's share of valid second votes nationwide, not an unspecified total of first and second votes. Under the Federal Constitutional Court's 30 July 2024 ruling on the 2023 electoral reform, a party below 5% was excluded from proportional seat allocation only if its candidates led the first votes in fewer than three constituencies. Thus at least three constituency first-place results could preserve participation in proportional allocation despite a sub-5% second-vote share. Parties representing national minorities were exempt from the threshold. The first vote supports a constituency candidate; the second vote determines party strength in allocation. Under the reformed second-vote-coverage system, a first-place constituency result is not invariably a guaranteed personal seat. The rule is intended to balance representation and parliamentary effectiveness; it does not establish that every small party is extremist. Do not apply this Bundestag rule automatically to state or European elections. Check the law and court decisions for the election date, since thresholds and seat-allocation rules can change.
groups.mid: At the 2025 Bundestag election, the 5% threshold used valid second votes nationwide. It did not combine both votes. The first vote supports a local constituency candidate. The second vote determines party strength in seat allocation. A Federal Constitutional Court ruling on 30 July 2024 changed how the 2023 reform applied. A party below 5% was excluded from proportional seats only if its candidates led the first votes in fewer than three constituencies. Winning the most first votes in at least three could therefore keep the party in proportional allocation. National-minority parties were exempt from the threshold. Under the reformed second-vote-coverage system, a candidate coming first locally was not always guaranteed a personal seat. The threshold aims to balance representation and an effective parliament. It does not mean all small parties are extremist. These are Bundestag rules, not automatic rules for state or European elections. Check the legislation and court decisions for the specific election date, since rules can change.
groups.low: For the 2025 Bundestag election, 5% meant a share of valid second votes across Germany. It was not both votes added together. The first vote is for a local candidate. The second vote sets a party's strength for allocating seats. On 30 July 2024, the Federal Constitutional Court ruled on the 2023 reform. A party below 5% was left out of proportional seats only if it led the first votes in fewer than three constituencies. At least three first-place results could keep it in proportional seats. National-minority parties were exempt. The new system used second-vote coverage. Coming first locally did not always guarantee that candidate a seat. The threshold aims to balance fair representation with a parliament that can work. It does not make every small party extremist. Do not use this rule for all state or European elections. Check the law and court rulings for the election date. Rules can change.
groups.source_review: Checked Federal Returning Officer explanation of2024 ruling/2025 operation, second votes and minority exemption.
groups.notes: Added dated court qualification, corrected first/second-vote ambiguity and guaranteed direct-seat claim.

groups.high: Directive (EU) 2019/1937 protects qualifying reports of breaches in specified areas of Union law, including financial services, public procurement, product and transport safety, environmental protection, public health, consumer protection and personal-data privacy. Private legal entities with 50 or more workers generally need internal reporting channels; particular sectors can require them below that size, and public-sector exceptions depend on permitted national arrangements. Channels must protect confidentiality and allow diligent follow-up. Internal receipt should normally be acknowledged within seven days, with feedback within a reasonable period not exceeding three months from acknowledgement or expiry of the seven-day acknowledgement period. Feedback is not a guarantee that every investigation is completed by that date. External reporting may be used without first reporting internally; public disclosure has additional conditions. Protection generally requires reasonable grounds to believe the information was true and within scope when reported. Motive alone does not remove protection; knowingly false reporting is different. Retaliation, including dismissal, demotion, harassment and threats, is prohibited. Anonymous-report handling, remedies and procedures depend on national implementation; the directive does not universally require every organisation to accept anonymous reports.
groups.mid: EU Directive 2019/1937 protects some reports of breaches of EU law. The report must meet its conditions. Its scope includes finance and public procurement. It covers product and transport safety, the environment, health, consumers and data privacy too. Private legal bodies with 50 or more workers usually need a way to report inside. Some sectors need them below that size too. Exceptions for public bodies depend on allowed national rules. Keep reports confidential. Follow them up with care. Normally acknowledge receipt of an internal report within seven days. Feedback is due in a reasonable time. It must be within three months of acknowledgement. If none was sent, count from the end of the seven-day period. Feedback does not mean every investigation must be complete then. A person can report externally without first reporting inside. Public disclosure has extra conditions. The person must usually have reasonable grounds for believing the facts. They must think the facts are true and in scope when reported. Personal motive alone does not remove protection. Knowingly false reports are different. Retaliation is banned, including dismissal, demotion, harassment and threats. National law sets details on anonymous reports, remedies and procedures. The directive does not make every body accept anonymous reports.
groups.low: EU Directive 2019/1937 protects some reports of breaches of EU law. It covers finance and public procurement, which means buying by public bodies. It covers safety, the environment and health too. Consumer rights and data privacy are also in scope. Private legal bodies with 50 or more workers usually need a way to report inside. Some sectors need one below that size. Exceptions for public bodies depend on allowed national rules. Keep reports confidential. Follow them up with care. Normally confirm you got an internal report within seven days. Give feedback within a reasonable time. The limit is three months from that reply. If none was sent, count from the end of the seven-day period. Not every investigation must be finished then. People can report to an outside authority first. Going public has extra conditions. The person usually needs good grounds to think the facts were true. They must think they are in scope at the time. A personal motive alone does not remove protection. Knowingly false reports are different. Retaliation is banned. This means harm for reporting. Examples are dismissal, demotion, harassment and threats. National law sets details on reports without names, remedies and procedures. There is no rule that every body must accept a report without a name.
groups.source_review: Checked directive text on scope,50workers,7days/3months, external reports and conditions for protection; direct HTML challenged but official PDF/search available.
groups.notes: Corrected10day acknowledgement, fabricated assessment/investigation timelines, blanket anonymity/public-body rules and motive-based exclusion.

groups.high: ICCPR Article 19 protects freedom of opinion and the freedom to seek, receive and impart information and ideas across borders and media. Holding an opinion is protected without interference. Restrictions on expression under Article 19(3) must be provided by accessible, sufficiently precise law and necessary and proportionate to a permitted aim: respect for others' rights or reputations, or protection of national security, public order, public health or morals. A lawful label alone is insufficient; authorities must explain the specific risk and why less restrictive measures would not adequately address it. Criticism of officials or unpopular ideas is not by itself a legitimate reason for suppression. General Comment 34 stresses narrow interpretation and protection against arbitrary discretion. Morals-based limits cannot rest exclusively on one social or religious tradition. Article 20 separately requires legal prohibition of war propaganda and advocacy of national, racial or religious hatred constituting incitement to discrimination, hostility or violence, consistently with Article 19 safeguards. National law and remedies determine how a particular interference is challenged; this framework does not endorse every defamation, insult or national-security offence.
groups.mid: ICCPR Article 19 protects your opinion and the right to seek, receive and share ideas. It covers borders and different forms of media. You must be free to hold an opinion without interference. Limits on expression need strict checks. Article 19(3) says the law must be clear and accessible. The limit must be necessary and proportionate. It must serve an allowed aim: other people's rights or reputation, national security, public order, public health or morals. Naming an aim is not enough. The state must show the risk and why a less restrictive step will not do. Criticism of officials or an unpopular view is not enough to justify a ban. General Comment 34 says limits should be narrow and not arbitrary. Morals cannot come only from one social or religious tradition. Article 20 also requires bans on war propaganda and advocacy of national, racial or religious hatred that incites discrimination, hostility or violence. Article 19 safeguards still apply. Local law affects how to challenge a limit. Not every insult, defamation or security offence is justified.
groups.low: ICCPR Article 19 protects opinions. It also protects the right to seek, receive and share ideas. This covers borders and different media. You must be free to hold a view without interference. Limits on what you say need strict checks. Article 19(3) requires a clear, accessible law. The limit must be needed. It must go no further than needed for its aim. It must serve an allowed aim. One aim is other people's rights or reputation. Others are national security and public order. Public health or morals are allowed aims too. Naming an aim is not enough. The state must show the risk. It must show why a step that limits less speech will not do. Criticism of officials is not itself a reason to ban speech. Nor is an unpopular view. General Comment 34 says limits must be narrow. They must not give officials a free choice to silence people. Morals cannot be based only on one social or religious tradition. Article 20 requires bans on war propaganda. It also covers calls for national, racial or religious hatred. To meet this rule, they must incite discrimination, hostility or violence. Article 19 safeguards still apply. Local law affects how you challenge a limit. The rules do not justify every law against insults or defamation. Nor do they justify every offence called a security offence.
groups.source_review: Checked General Comment34 and Article19/20 framework; treaty landing page403 but official comment available.
groups.notes: Separated opinion from expression, corrected indiscriminate insult/defamation approval and qualified necessity formula.

groups.high: UK parliamentary candidate spending is not governed by a universal £30,000 constituency cap. For the 2024 general election short campaign in Great Britain, Electoral Commission guidance specified £11,390 plus 12 pence per registered parliamentary elector in a county constituency, or plus 8 pence in a borough constituency (burgh in Scotland). The relevant electorate was measured on the last date for publication of the election notice. A county seat with 72,021 electors therefore had a £20,032.52 limit. There was no long campaign for that election. Candidate limits differ from political-party campaign limits, and other elections or periods can have different rules. The Representation of the People Act 1983 and amending rules govern candidate spending, authorisation, records and returns. Spending includes regulated goods and services used for the campaign, not necessarily every personal or exempt cost. Agents and candidates must track attributable spending, invoices and donations and meet return/declaration deadlines. Breaches can be offences, but penalties or disqualification depend on the facts and legal process. Check current election-specific guidance rather than applying a historical amount mechanically.
groups.mid: There is no universal £30,000 spending cap for a UK parliamentary candidate. For the 2024 short campaign in Great Britain, the limit was a fixed £11,390 plus an amount per registered parliamentary elector. Add 12p for each elector in a county constituency, or 8p in a borough constituency, called a burgh in Scotland. Use the electorate on the last date for publishing the election notice. For example, 72,021 electors in a county seat gave a limit of £20,032.52. There was no long campaign in that election. Candidate limits are separate from a political party's campaign limit. Other elections or periods may use other rules. The Representation of the People Act 1983 and amendments cover candidate spending, authorisation, records and returns. Costs count according to the rules for campaign goods and services; not all personal or exempt spending counts. Candidates and agents should keep invoices and donation records and meet return and declaration deadlines. A breach can be an offence, but penalties or disqualification require the relevant facts and process. Check guidance for the exact election date.
groups.low: There is no fixed £30,000 cap for all candidates for the UK Parliament. In the 2024 short campaign in Great Britain, start with £11,390. For a county constituency, add 12p for each registered parliamentary elector. Add 8p in a borough constituency, or burgh in Scotland. Use the voter count on the last date for publishing the election notice. A county seat with 72,021 electors had a £20,032.52 limit. There was no long campaign that year. A party's spending limit is separate. Other elections and periods can use other rules. The Representation of the People Act 1983 covers this. Later amendments changed the rules. The rules cover spending and approval. They cover records and returns too. Check which campaign goods and services count. Not all personal or exempt costs count. Candidates and agents must keep invoices and donation records. Send returns and declarations on time. A breach can be an offence. Fines or disqualification depend on the case. The legal process must be followed. Read the guide for the exact election. Do not use one old figure for all cases.
groups.source_review: Checked EC exact2024 formula and worked example, corroborated statutory2023 adjustment. A separate EC press page reverses pence labels, so relied on detailed guidance/statute.
groups.notes: Corrected universal£30000 cap and automatic disqualification; specified election/year/geography and county/borough rates.

groups.high: Under the 1951 Refugee Convention and 1967 Protocol, a refugee is generally outside their country of nationality and unable or, owing to well-founded fear, unwilling to use that country's protection because of persecution linked to race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion. Stateless persons are assessed with reference to their former habitual residence. Refugee status determination evaluates the facts, country conditions and applicable law; past persecution, attributed beliefs and non-state persecutors can be relevant. A person need not prove they were uniquely singled out where a group faces persecution. Conflict may produce Convention persecution or qualify under broader regional or complementary protection rules. Internal relocation, protection availability, exclusion and cessation require careful legal assessment; absence of national protection does not automatically decide all of them. Evidence should be assessed fairly, recognising that fleeing people may lack documents. Individual procedures are common, but prima facie group recognition is legitimate in appropriate mass-arrival situations. Non-refoulement prohibits return to relevant danger under applicable law; the Convention's provision has specified exceptions, while other human-rights protections may prohibit removal independently. Seek qualified advice for an individual claim.
groups.mid: A refugee claim uses the 1951 Refugee Convention and 1967 Protocol. A person is generally outside their country. They cannot, or because of a well-founded fear will not, seek its protection. The persecution must be linked to race, religion, nationality, a particular social group or political opinion. For a stateless person, look at the country where they used to live habitually. Officials check personal facts, country conditions and the law. Past harm, views wrongly attributed to someone and threats from non-state groups can matter. You do not have to be the only person targeted if your group faces persecution. War may involve this kind of harm or other regional or complementary protection. Safe relocation, state protection, exclusion and when status ends all need checks. Lack of state protection does not settle everything alone. People fleeing may lack papers. Their evidence needs fair assessment. Individual cases are common, but prima facie group recognition can be used for some mass arrivals. Non-refoulement protects against return to danger under relevant law. The Convention has exceptions; other human-rights rules may still stop removal. Get qualified advice for your own case.
groups.low: The 1951 Refugee Convention and 1967 Protocol set the main test. The person is usually outside their country. They cannot get its protection. Or they will not seek it due to a well-founded fear. The feared harm is persecution for a set reason. There are five reasons: race, religion, nationality, a particular social group or political opinion. For a stateless person, look at the former habitual residence. This is the country where they used to live. Officials check personal facts, country conditions and law. Past harm can matter. So can views people wrongly think the person holds. Groups outside the state can cause persecution too. You need not be the only person targeted if your group faces persecution. War may involve this harm. Other regional or complementary protection may apply too. These are other routes to safety under the law. Could the person safely live elsewhere in their country? Can the state protect them? Could an exclusion rule apply, or could status end? Check each issue. Lack of state protection alone does not settle all of them. People fleeing may lack papers. Assess evidence fairly. Individual cases are common. In some mass arrivals, the whole group can be recognised on clear facts. This is called prima facie group recognition. Non-refoulement is the rule against return to relevant danger. The Convention has exceptions. Other human-rights law may still stop removal. Get qualified advice for your own case.
groups.source_review: Checked UNHCR definition, stateless application and prima facie guidance; non-refoulement qualification retained.
groups.notes: Corrected all-individual/no-group claim, uniquely-targeted test, balance-of-probabilities standard, automatic no-relocation and absolute Convention33 claim.

groups.high: The United Nations Convention against Corruption (UNCAC) was adopted on 31 October 2003 and entered into force on 14 December 2005. It addresses prevention, criminalisation, international cooperation and asset recovery; there is no separate treaty-wide Anti-Corruption Declaration imposing identical filing duties on all officials. Article 8(5) calls on states to endeavour, where appropriate and consistent with domestic law, to establish systems for officials to declare outside activities, employment, investments, assets and substantial gifts or benefits that may create conflicts of interest. Article 52(5) calls for consideration of effective financial-disclosure systems for appropriate officials, with sanctions for non-compliance where applicable. Article 52(6) concerns considering reporting duties for relevant foreign financial-account interests. These provisions are qualified and do not universally mandate public annual declarations by every official. Domestic law determines coverage, thresholds, frequency, verification, confidentiality, publication and penalties. Declarations can reveal conflicts or unexplained wealth, but a discrepancy alone does not prove corruption; fair investigation matters. Party counts change: the UN depositary listed 192 parties on 10 September 2026, not a timeless 190 states. Check current treaty status and the applicable national regime.
groups.mid: UNCAC is the United Nations Convention against Corruption. It was adopted on 31 October 2003 and took effect on 14 December 2005. It covers prevention, crimes, work across countries and recovery of assets. It does not have one separate Anti-Corruption Declaration that sets the same filing rule for all officials. Article 8(5) asks states to try, where appropriate under their law, to set up declarations. These cover outside activities, jobs, investments, assets and large gifts or benefits that may cause conflicts of interest. Article 52(5) says to consider financial-disclosure systems for suitable officials and sanctions where applicable. Article 52(6) says to consider reports of certain interests in foreign bank accounts. These duties have limits. They do not mean every official must publish a report each year. National law decides who reports, what counts, dates, checks, privacy, public access and penalties. A report may reveal a conflict or unexplained wealth. A mismatch alone does not prove a crime. Check it fairly. The UN listed 192 parties on 10 September 2026, not a permanent 190. Check current treaty status and local law.
groups.low: UNCAC means United Nations Convention against Corruption. It was adopted on 31 October 2003. It took effect on 14 December 2005. It covers ways to prevent and punish corruption. It also covers work across countries and recovery of assets. There is no separate Anti-Corruption Declaration that makes all officials file the same report. Article 8(5) asks states to try to set up declarations. They should do so where appropriate under their own law. These cover outside work, jobs, investments and assets. They also cover large gifts or benefits. These may cause conflicts of interest. Article 52(5) says to consider financial-disclosure systems for suitable officials. This means reporting what they own and their financial interests. Sanctions may apply where appropriate. Article 52(6) says to consider reports of certain interests in foreign accounts. These duties have limits. They do not make all officials publish yearly reports. National law sets who reports and what counts. It sets dates and checks too. It sets privacy, public access and penalties. A report may show a conflict or wealth with no clear source. A mismatch alone does not prove a crime. Check it fairly. The UN listed 192 parties on 10 September 2026. The old 190 figure is not fixed. Check the treaty's current status. Check local law too.
groups.source_review: Checked official treaty publication/UNODC review qualifications and UN depositary September2026 count. UNODC legacy treaty URL404; official state treaty publication used.
groups.notes: Corrected adoption month, invented separate declaration/universal public annual mandate, unqualified party count and guilt-by-discrepancy implication.
